mcqs.q: Pathology is defined as the scientific study of:
opts: Disease — the structural, biochemical and functional changes in cells, tissues and organs
mcqs.explain: Pathology (pathos = suffering, logos = study) studies the structural, biochemical and functional changes in cells, tissues and organs in disease.

mcqs.q: The study of the NORMAL functions of cells is called:
mcqs.explain: Physiology studies normal cell function; pathology studies the diseased/damaged cell and its altered function.

mcqs.q: Etiology refers to the:
opts: Cause or origin of a disease
mcqs.explain: Etiology (aetiology) is the cause/origin of a disease — either genetic (intrinsic) or acquired (extrinsic).

mcqs.q: An inherited mutation is classed as which type of etiology?
mcqs.explain: Genetic/intrinsic causes include inherited mutations and chromosomal abnormalities; acquired/extrinsic causes include infection, chemicals, trauma and nutrition.

mcqs.q: Pathogenesis describes the:
opts: Mechanism / sequence of events from the initial stimulus to the disease
mcqs.explain: Pathogenesis is the chain/mechanism of events leading from the initial stimulus to the ultimate expression of the disease.

mcqs.q: A 'lesion' is best defined as:
opts: A structural alteration in tissue due to disease (e.g. ulcer, leukoplakia)
mcqs.explain: A lesion is a structural alteration in tissues caused by disease — examples include an ulcer, leukoplakia or a tumour mass.

mcqs.q: Morphological changes visible to the NAKED EYE are termed:
mcqs.explain: Gross/macroscopic changes are visible to the naked eye; microscopic changes are seen under the light/electron microscope.

mcqs.q: Changes seen only under the microscope are:
mcqs.explain: Microscopic changes are structural alterations seen with the light or electron microscope (histopathology).

mcqs.q: A 'sign' in pathology is:
opts: Objective evidence observed by the doctor (e.g. swelling, redness)
A sensation felt only by the patient
A group of features occurring together
mcqs.explain: A sign is objective evidence the doctor can observe (swelling, redness); a symptom is subjective (felt by the patient).

mcqs.q: Pain and burning experienced by the patient are examples of:
mcqs.explain: Symptoms are subjective experiences reported by the patient (e.g. pain, burning); signs are objective and observed by the doctor.

mcqs.q: A group of signs and symptoms that occur together (e.g. Down's syndrome) is a:
mcqs.explain: A syndrome is a group of signs and symptoms that occur together, such as Down's syndrome.

mcqs.q: A 'provisional diagnosis' is:
opts: The most likely working diagnosis made before confirmatory investigations
A list of all possible diseases
mcqs.explain: A provisional diagnosis is the most likely working diagnosis before confirmatory tests; the differential is the list of possibilities.

mcqs.q: A 'differential diagnosis' is:
opts: A list of possible diseases with similar features
mcqs.explain: A differential diagnosis is the list of possible diseases that share similar clinical features.

mcqs.q: Prognosis is the:
opts: Prediction of the outcome of a disease (good or poor)
mcqs.explain: Prognosis predicts the outcome — e.g. mild dysplastic leukoplakia has a better prognosis than oral cancer.

mcqs.q: General pathology deals with:
opts: Basic mechanisms common to all diseases (cell injury, inflammation, healing)
Diseases of one specific organ only
mcqs.explain: General pathology covers the basic mechanisms common across all tissues — cell injury, necrosis, inflammation, repair and circulatory disturbances.

mcqs.q: Systemic pathology studies:
mcqs.explain: Systemic pathology applies general principles to specific organs/systems (cardiovascular, respiratory, GI, etc.).

mcqs.q: The branch most directly relevant to dentistry is:
mcqs.explain: Oral pathology focuses on the oral cavity, jaws, salivary glands and maxillofacial region — directly relevant to dentistry.

mcqs.q: Haematology, clinical chemistry, microbiology and cytology are subdivisions of:
mcqs.explain: Clinical pathology / laboratory medicine includes haematology, clinical chemistry, microbiology and cytology.

mcqs.q: Forensic pathology deals with:
opts: Medico-legal aspects of disease and death
mcqs.explain: Forensic pathology addresses the medico-legal aspects of disease and death (like crime investigation).

mcqs.q: Fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) belongs to which subdivision?
mcqs.explain: Cytology, including exfoliative cytology and FNAC, is a subdivision of clinical/laboratory pathology.

mcqs.q: Which sequence correctly describes what pathology studies in a disease?
opts: Etiology → pathogenesis → morphological changes → clinical features
mcqs.explain: Pathology studies a disease via its etiology (cause), pathogenesis (mechanism), morphological changes and resulting clinical features.

mcqs.q: The fundamental structural and functional unit studied in pathology is the:
mcqs.explain: The cell is the basic unit of the body (cells → tissues → organs → bodies); pathology studies the diseased cell.

saqs.q: Define pathology and differentiate it from physiology.
saqs.a: Pathology = the study of disease (structural, biochemical, functional changes in cells/tissues/organs). Physiology = the study of normal cell function.
Etiology = the cause of a disease (genetic or acquired). Pathogenesis = the mechanism/chain of events from the stimulus to the disease.

saqs.q: Distinguish gross and microscopic morphological changes.
saqs.a: Gross/macroscopic = visible to the naked eye (swelling, ulcer). Microscopic = seen under the light/electron microscope.

saqs.q: Differentiate a sign, a symptom and a syndrome.
saqs.a: Sign = objective, observed by the doctor. Symptom = subjective, felt by the patient. Syndrome = a group of signs and symptoms occurring together.
Clinical, provisional, differential, laboratory/histopathological, and final diagnosis.
General, systemic, oral, clinical (laboratory), and forensic pathology.

saqs.q: What is prognosis? Give an oral example.
saqs.a: Prognosis = the prediction of disease outcome. E.g. mild dysplastic leukoplakia has a better prognosis than oral cancer.
